docs.title: GraphEasy Language
docs.text:
GraphEasy is an efficient, easy-to-use DSL for describing graphs and writing graph algorithms. Programs are written in .graph files, compiled by GraphProgram, and linked with a C++ runtime.

  • Repo: https://github.com/nash-raf/Graph-language-
  • Getting Started: See Getting Started

docs.title: What you can do
docs.text:
• Load graphs from an edgelist file or define them inline
  • Run built-in graph queries (BFS, DFS, Dijkstra, and more)
  • Write custom algorithms with for each loops over vertices, edges, neighbors, or sets
  • Use arrays, sets, conditionals, and while-loops in a C-like syntax
  • Filter and combine graphs with graph comprehensions

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
graph G {
  edges: file 'edgelist.txt';
};

query path : "bfs" of G;
print path;

docs.title: Running a program (p2GraphEasy)
docs.text:
From the p2GraphEasy directory:

./1run.sh test.graph test.graph   # compile GraphProgram + your program
./2final_run.sh                   # link and run

See Grammar for syntax, Algorithms for complete benchmark programs, and Bron-Kerbosch for a recursive maximal-clique example.

docs.title: Algorithms
docs.text: This page lists the five aligned algorithms used in the benchmark suite.

docs.title: BFS Parent
docs.text:
BFS parent computes a breadth-first traversal tree from source vertex 0. Each discovered vertex stores the vertex that first reached it.

graph G {
  edges: file "graph.txt";
};

int n = numVertices(G);
int visited[n];
int parent[n];
int frontier[n];
int next_frontier[n];
int frontier_size = 1;
int next_size = 0;
int init_i = 0;

while (init_i < n) {
  visited[init_i] = 0;
  parent[init_i] = -1;
  init_i = init_i + 1;
}

frontier[0] = 0;
visited[0] = 1;
parent[0] = 0;

while (frontier_size > 0) {
  next_size = 0;
  int i = 0;

  while (i < frontier_size) {
    int v = frontier[i];
    for each neighbor u of v in G {
      if (visited[u] == 0) {
        visited[u] = 1;
        parent[u] = v;
        next_frontier[next_size] = u;
        next_size = next_size + 1;
      }
    }
    i = i + 1;
  }

  swap(frontier, next_frontier);
  frontier_size = next_size;
}

docs.title: Connected Components
docs.text:
Connected components uses label propagation. Each vertex starts with its own id, then lower labels spread through the graph until convergence.

graph G {
  edges: file "graph.txt";
};

int n = numVertices(G);
int id[n];
set frontier;
set next;

for each vertex v in G {
  id[v] = v;
}

frontier = G.nodes;

while (setSize(frontier) > 0) {
  next = {};
  for each element u in frontier {
    for each neighbor v of u in G {
      if (id[u] < id[v]) {
        id[v] = id[u];
        next.add(v);
      }
    }
  }
  frontier = next;
}

docs.title: KCore
docs.text:
KCore removes vertices whose degree is below k. Removing a vertex reduces the degree of its live neighbors, which may create more removals.

graph G {
  edges: file "graph.txt";
};

int n = numVertices(G);
int k = 5;
int deg[n];
int alive[n];
set frontier;
set next;

for each vertex v in G {
  deg[v] = 0;
  alive[v] = 1;
}

for each vertex u in G {
  for each neighbor v of u in G {
    deg[u] = deg[u] + 1;
  }
}

frontier = {};
for each vertex v in G {
  if (deg[v] < k) {
    frontier.add(v);
  }
}

while (setSize(frontier) > 0) {
  next = {};
  for each element u in frontier {
    if (alive[u] == 1) {
      alive[u] = 0;
      for each neighbor v of u in G {
        if (alive[v] == 1) {
          deg[v] = deg[v] - 1;
          if (deg[v] < k) {
            next.add(v);
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
  frontier = next;
}

docs.title: PageRank
docs.text:
PageRank runs fixed-count power iteration. The benchmark uses damping factor 0.85, 20 iterations, and outgoing adjacency.

graph G {
  edges: file "graph.txt";
};

int n = numVertices(G);
real damp = 0.85;
real one_over_n = 1.0 / n;
real beta = (1.0 - damp) / n;
real cur_rank[n];
real next_rank[n];
int out_degree[n];
int round = 0;
int max_rounds = 20;

for each vertex v in G {
  cur_rank[v] = one_over_n;
  next_rank[v] = beta;
  out_degree[v] = 0;
}

for each vertex u in G {
  out_degree[u] = outDegree(G, u);
}

while (round < max_rounds) {
  round = round + 1;

  for each vertex v in G {
    next_rank[v] = beta;
  }

  for each vertex u in G {
    int outd = out_degree[u];
    if (outd > 0) {
      real contrib = damp * cur_rank[u] / outd;
      for each out neighbor v of u in G {
        next_rank[v] = next_rank[v] + contrib;
      }
    }
  }

  for each vertex v in G {
    cur_rank[v] = next_rank[v];
  }
}

docs.title: SSSP
docs.text:
SSSP uses a frontier-based Bellman-Ford style relaxation over a weighted graph.

graph G {
  edges: file "weighted_graph.txt";
  TRUE
};

int n = numVertices(G);
int inf = 2147483647;
int dist[n];
set frontier;
set next;
int src = 0;
int rounds = 0;

for each vertex v in G {
  dist[v] = inf;
}

dist[src] = 0;
frontier = {0};

while (setSize(frontier) > 0) {
  if (rounds == n) {
    print "negative cycle";
    break;
  }

  next = {};
  for each element u in frontier {
    if (dist[u] != inf) {
      for each neighbor v of u in G {
        int nd = dist[u] + weight(G, u, v);
        if (nd < dist[v]) {
          dist[v] = nd;
          next.add(v);
        }
      }
    }
  }
  frontier = next;
  rounds = rounds + 1;
}

docs.title: Bron-Kerbosch Maximal-Clique Search
docs.text: Bron-Kerbosch is a recursive backtracking algorithm that enumerates every maximal clique in an undirected graph. This example shows how GraphEasy combines functions, sets, graph comprehensions, and recursion to describe the algorithm directly.

docs.title: Algorithm State
docs.text:
Each recursive call maintains three vertex sets:

Set Meaning R Vertices already included in the current clique P Candidate vertices that can still extend the clique X Previously considered vertices, used to avoid duplicate maximal cliques

A clique is maximal when both P and X are empty. At that point, no remaining or previously processed vertex can extend R.

docs.title: Describing A Neighborhood
docs.text:
The helper function creates a graph view containing the edges incident to vertex v, obtains its vertices, and removes v itself:

fn set neighborsOf(graph G, int v) {
    graph H = [G where edge has v];
    set Nv = H.vertices;
    Nv.remove(v);
    return Nv;
}

The expression edge has v selects edges incident to v. The resulting H.vertices set therefore contains v and all its neighbors.

docs.title: Candidate Refinement
docs.text:
For each candidate vertex v, the algorithm adds it to the current clique and intersects the remaining candidate sets with its neighborhood:

set R_new = R;
R_new.add(v);

set P_new = P intersect Nv;
set X_new = X intersect Nv;

graph H = [G where vertex in P_new];
bronKerbosch(H, R_new, P_new, X_new);

P intersect Nv keeps only candidates adjacent to v, so every vertex passed to the recursive call remains connected to every vertex in the growing clique. The graph comprehension gives the recursive call a candidate-focused vertex view while preserving the graph's vertex identifiers.

After recursion, v moves from P to X:

P.remove(v);
X.add(v);

This prevents the same maximal clique from being reported through a different candidate order.

docs.title: Complete GraphEasy Program
docs.text:
fn set neighborsOf(graph G, int v) {
    graph H = [G where edge has v];
    set Nv = H.vertices;
    Nv.remove(v);
    return Nv;
}

fn int bronKerbosch(graph G, set R, set P, set X) {
    if (P.size() == 0 && X.size() == 0) {
        print "maximal clique";
        print R.size();
        return 0;
    }

    set P_work = P;

    while (P_work.size() > 0) {
        int v = P_work.pop();
        set Nv = neighborsOf(G, v);

        set R_new = R;
        R_new.add(v);

        set P_new = P intersect Nv;
        set X_new = X intersect Nv;

        graph H = [G where vertex in P_new];
        bronKerbosch(H, R_new, P_new, X_new);

        P.remove(v);
        X.add(v);
    }

    return 0;
}

graph G {
    nodes: 0, 1, 2, 3;
    edges: 0->1, 1->2, 0->2, 2->3;
};

set R = {};
set P = G.nodes;
set X = {};

bronKerbosch(G, R, P, X);

docs.title: Example Result
docs.text:
The example graph contains the triangle {0, 1, 2} and the maximal edge clique {2, 3}. The program reports their sizes:

maximal clique
2
maximal clique
3

The implementation was also tested on a 40-edge graph against an independent Python Bron-Kerbosch implementation. Both produced maximal-clique sizes 4, 4, 5, 8.

docs.title: Grammar
docs.text: This page summarizes the language syntax used by GraphEasy programs. The first part follows the core grammar in Base.g4; the second part documents extensions used by the benchmark programs.

docs.title: Program Structure
docs.text:
A program is a sequence of statements and function definitions:

program: (statement | function)* EOF;

Statements include graph definitions, variable declarations, conditionals, loops, graph comprehensions, queries, graph display, graph mutation, function calls, and print statements.

docs.title: Graph Definitions
docs.text:
Graphs are declared with the graph keyword:

graph G {
  nodes: 0, 1, 2, 3;
  edges: 0->1, 1->2, 2->3;
};

Graphs can also load edges from a file:

graph G {
  edges: file "edgelist.txt";
};

Graphs are undirected by default. Add directed:true; inside the graph block to preserve edge direction:

graph G {
  directed:true;
  edges: file "directed_edgelist.txt";
};

For a directed graph, an input line u v creates only u -> v. Without directed:true;, GraphEasy treats that line as an undirected edge and builds both adjacency directions.

Weighted input is used by the benchmark runtime with TRUE inside the graph block:

graph G {
  edges: file "weighted_edgelist.txt";
  TRUE
};

docs.title: Types And Variables
docs.text:
Core scalar types are:

Type Meaning int Integer real Floating-point value bool Boolean string String vertex Vertex value edge Edge value graph Graph value

Examples:

int source = 0;
real damping = 0.85;
bool active = true;
string label = "bfs";

docs.title: Expressions
docs.text:
The core expression grammar supports arithmetic, function calls, identifiers, integers, reals, booleans, and parentheses:

int x = 2 + 3 * 4;
real y = (1.0 - damping) / n;
int z = numVertices(G);

Comparison and logical operators are used in conditions:

if (dist[v] > dist[u] + w) {
  dist[v] = dist[u] + w;
}

if (a < b && b < c) {
  print "ordered";
}

docs.title: Loops
docs.text:
GraphEasy has while loops:

while (round < max_rounds) {
  round = round + 1;
}

It also has graph traversal loops:

for each vertex v in G {
  print v;
}

for each edge u, v in G {
  print u;
}

for each neighbor v of u in G {
  print v;
}

for each out neighbor v of u in G {
  print v;
}

for each in neighbor v of u in G {
  print v;
}

On undirected graphs, neighbor, out neighbor, and in neighbor traverse the same adjacency. On directed graphs, neighbor and out neighbor traverse outgoing edges, while in neighbor traverses incoming edges.

docs.title: Graph Queries
docs.text:
Built-in graph queries use this form:

query result : "bfs" of G;
print result;

The grammar accepts a string query name. Runtime support determines which query strings are implemented.

docs.title: Graph Comprehension
docs.text:
Graph comprehensions filter an existing graph:

H = [G where degree > 2];
K = [G where degree > 2 && connected with 0];

Supported graph conditions include degree comparisons, connectivity with a vertex, logical &&, logical ||, and parentheses.

docs.title: Graph Mutation
docs.text:
Nodes and edges can be added to or removed from a graph:

add 4 to G;
add 2->4 to G;
remove 0->1 from G;

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
Functions have a return type, name, parameter list, and block:

fn int add_one(int x) {
  return x + 1;
}

int y = add_one(4);

docs.title: Print And Show
docs.text:
print "done";
print x;
print edges of G;
print nodes of G;
print graph of G;
show G;

docs.title: Benchmark Extensions
docs.text: The benchmark algorithms use implementation features beyond the minimal Base.g4 listing.

docs.title: Arrays
docs.text:
int n = numVertices(G);
int parent[n];
real rank[n];

parent[0] = 0;
rank[0] = 1.0 / n;

docs.title: Sets
docs.text:
set frontier;
set next;

frontier = {0};
next = {};
next.add(v);

while (setSize(frontier) > 0) {
  frontier = next;
}

docs.title: Set Traversal
docs.text:
for each element u in frontier {
  print u;
}

docs.title: Runtime Helpers
docs.text:
Common helper calls in benchmark programs:

Helper Use numVertices(G) Number of vertices numEdges(G) Logical edge count; directed graphs are not divided by two degree(G, v) Undirected degree, or inDegree + outDegree on directed graphs outDegree(G, v) Outgoing degree inDegree(G, v) Incoming degree hasEdge(G, u, v) Direction-sensitive edge lookup on directed graphs weight(G, u, v) Edge weight for weighted SSSP setSize(frontier) Number of elements in a set swap(a, b) Swap array-backed frontier buffers

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This page shows the smallest path from a .graph file to a running GraphEasy program.

docs.title: Minimal Program
docs.text:
graph G {
  edges: file "edgelist.txt";
};

query path : "bfs" of G;
print path;

The graph file is a plain edgelist. For an unweighted graph, each line contains two integer vertex ids:

0 1
1 2
1 3
2 4

GraphEasy loads graphs as undirected unless the graph block says otherwise:

graph G {
  directed:true;
  edges: file "directed_edgelist.txt";
};

In a directed graph, neighbor means outgoing neighbor. Use in neighbor, out neighbor, inDegree, and outDegree when direction matters.

For a weighted graph, each line contains source destination weight:

0 1 7
1 2 3
2 4 5

docs.title: Run A Program
docs.text:
From a GraphEasy implementation directory such as p2GraphEasy:

./1run.sh test.graph test.graph
./2final_run.sh

The first command compiles the language frontend and the .graph program. The second command links the generated objects with the runtime and executes the final binary.

docs.title: Project Layout
docs.text:
The repository has multiple implementation families:

Directory Purpose p1GraphEasy Baseline GraphEasy implementation p2GraphEasy Optimized GraphEasy implementation p1GraphEasy-con-AutoTuner P1 with autotuner support p2GraphEasy-con-AutoTuner P2 with autotuner support
